title: Raw Pointers

writing.exampleCaption: Creating the pointer from `&value` is safe; the `unsafe` block covers only the read, while `value` is alive.
writing.explanation:
Creating `*const T` or `*mut T` is safe; dereferencing one is `unsafe` because validity, alignment, initialization, and aliasing are now the programmer's proof obligations.

A raw pointer such as `*const T` or `*mut T` can represent a location without the safety guarantees that a normal Rust reference carries. Constructing one from a valid reference is safe. Dereferencing it requires `unsafe` because the compiler cannot prove that the pointed-to object is still alive, aligned, initialized, in bounds, and accessed under valid aliasing rules. A raw pointer may carry provenance information about its allocation; treating it as merely a numeric address can miss part of the memory model.

In the example, `pointer` is created from `&value`, and `value` remains alive while the pointer is read. That local reasoning supports the `unsafe` dereference. Change the example conceptually so the pointer outlives `value`; now the proof fails even if the numeric address still looks plausible. Never use a runtime test as proof that dereferencing an invalid pointer is safe: undefined behavior may appear to work once. Keep the `unsafe` operation close to the checks that justify it, and expose a safe API only when callers cannot violate those assumptions. For FFI, additionally document who owns the allocation and when the foreign side may retain or free the pointer.

Pointer arithmetic adds more obligations: an offset must stay within the permitted allocation rules even if it is not dereferenced immediately. Do not infer validity from a non-null address alone. Prefer slices, references, and `NonNull`-based library APIs when they express the invariant safely; a raw pointer is useful at FFI and data-structure internals, where its proof can be tightly contained.
writing.feedback: Creating and printing the pointer are safe, since neither touches the memory behind it. Only the dereference needs `unsafe`, and here its proof fails.
writing.question: Which operation needs `unsafe`?

writing.task: Decide which lines need `unsafe`. Then explain why the commented-out read would be undefined behaviour even if it happened to print 7. Do not run it as proof.

recall.question: This compiles. What is wrong with it?
recall.answer: A raw pointer carries no lifetime, so the borrow checker doesn't object when it outlives `value`. But `value` is gone, so the dereference is undefined behaviour, even if it happens to print 7. The `unsafe` block claims a validity proof that doesn't hold.

recall.question: Why is `ptr.add(1)` an `unsafe` method even though it reads no memory, while `ptr.wrapping_add(1)` is safe?
recall.answer: `add` requires the result to stay within the same allocation (or one past its end); violating that is undefined behaviour at once, so calling it without `unsafe` is E0133. `wrapping_add` makes no such promise and just computes an address; dereferencing either result is still `unsafe`.

illustration.alt: A raw pointer reaches memory only after allocation, alignment, initialization, bounds, and aliasing requirements are established.
illustration.caption: Unsafe dereference requires a concrete proof of the pointer invariants.
